references.text: Jesus had predicted that Peter would deny him three times before the rooster crowed ([ref:Luk 22:34|Luke 22:34]). Here begins the fulfillment of this prophecy as Peter denies knowing Jesus.
Matthew's parallel account of Peter's first denial, where he also denies to a servant girl and says he does not know what she is talking about ([ref:Matt 26:70|Matthew 26:70]).
Mark's parallel account of Peter's first denial, where he denies and says that he neither knows nor understands what the woman is saying ([ref:Mark 14:68|Mark 14:68]).
John's parallel account of Peter's first denial, where he says "No, I am not" when the servant girl asks if he is one of Jesus' disciples ([ref:Joh 18:17|John 18:17]).
The second denial follows shortly after, showing that Peter continues to deny knowing Jesus, just as Jesus had predicted ([ref:Luk 22:58|Luke 22:58]).

After the third denial, the Lord turned and looked at Peter, and Peter remembered the words of Jesus and went out and wept bitterly ([ref:Luk 22:61-62|Luke 22:61-62]). This shows the consequence of the denial that began in verse 57.
Paul writes that if we deny him, he will also deny us ([ref:2 Tim 2:12|2 Timothy 2:12]). Peter's denial is a serious example of what it means to deny Christ.
Jesus warned that whoever denies him before men, he will also deny before his Father in heaven ([ref:Matt 10:33|Matthew 10:33]). Peter's denial in Luke 22:57 is a direct illustration of this.

The prophecy about the Lord's suffering servant who was despised and forsaken by men ([ref:Jes 53:3|Isaiah 53:3]). Peter's denial is part of the fulfillment that Jesus was betrayed and abandoned, even by those closest to him.
